label: lr-84498
summary: The model predicts churn mainly from customer-service calls, daytime use, the voice-mail plan, the international plan and a few state offsets, added on the score. Many service calls raise the predicted risk once they close a hinge that daytime use holds open, so heavier daytime users need more calls (typical customer at 15 US dollars of daytime charge: 1.6% with 0 calls, 52.8% with 4 calls). The model is nearly flat in daytime charge up to a point and then rises steeply, much less so with a voice-mail plan (40.1% without and 2.1% with a plan at 45 US dollars). An international plan raises the score through its own edge (1.3% to 19.4% for the typical customer). Per-state offsets, largest for small states such as Hawaii (-3.69 on the score for 73 training customers), look fitted to small groups; night use matters mainly in Ohio, where the hinge that elsewhere cancels the direct night slope is pushed down.

overall_function: The network adds a handful of effects on the log-odds scale and passes the sum through a sigmoid. Customer-service calls raise the predicted churn risk through a threshold: they count only once they close a hinge that daytime use holds open, so the threshold rises with daytime use. Daytime use itself is nearly flat up to a point and then raises the risk steeply, mostly for customers without a voice-mail plan (the plan gates the serial chain that drives the rise); an international plan raises the risk by a fixed log-odds step that compounds with the others; evening use is non-monotone (a dip for heavy evening users, then a rise at the extreme through the daytime chain); night use matters mainly in Ohio. Per-state offsets (direct terms and single-state units) shift the score for about half the states; the model ignores voice-mail message counts, night calls, international minutes and charge, area codes 408 and 510, and the duplicate minutes/charge columns.
clinical_terms: In customer terms the model flags as likely to leave the customers who have called customer service many times (more calls needed the heavier their daytime use), the heaviest daytime users without a voice-mail plan, and customers with an international plan; these effects compound. A voice-mail plan protects heavy daytime users, very heavy evening use slightly lowers the risk except at the very top, and night use raises it mainly for customers in Ohio. Some states get large fixed offsets (Hawaii and Vermont lower, Washington and California higher) that look fitted to small groups rather than to a real regional pattern.
stuck: Little. The service-call leaf resists a single-concept reading (partial); a first hierarchy left a dead unit only as an entry, fixed by undoing the annotations and splitting the night chain; one-hot where-syntax took a retry.
